rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to observe all eight compounds and locate the elution window and critical pairs. A moderate temperature and 10-minute gradient provide a baseline for optimizing selectivity and run time.

Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to test temperature-driven selectivity in the crowded middle cluster and co-eluting final pair. The short initial elution window leaves ample room for later gradient flattening.

Flatten the gradient at the better-performing temperature to test whether the remaining close pairs gain separation. The current last peak at 5.08 minutes suggests substantial room to lengthen the gradient without a large time penalty.

The shallower gradient resolved the middle cluster but introduced a new co-elution. Lowering temperature by 5 °C tests selectivity for that pair, while shortening the gradient slightly helps keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

At 60 °C, an intermediate gradient duration may retain the improved middle-cluster separation while moving away from the co-elution seen at 24 minutes. This should also keep the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Shorten the gradient to improve the remaining late critical pair, whose resolution increased substantially from 24 to 20 minutes. This tests whether it can reach 1.5 before the middle pair loses full resolution.

Increase the starting organic fraction by one step to fine-tune selectivity and gradient slope near the nearly fully resolved method. This tests whether the middle pair can exceed R = 1.5 while preserving the late-pair separation and short elution time.

Slightly flatten the gradient from injection 7 by lowering the endpoint one step. This should improve both close middle pairs while using the late pair’s resolution margin, potentially bringing every pair to R ≥ 1.5.

This gives a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, between injections 7 and 8, targeting full resolution of both competing critical pairs. The last peak should elute before the gradient ends, so the lower endpoint should preserve the separation pattern.

Injection 9 reached the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark. Raise the starting organic fraction and slightly flatten the gradient to seek earlier elution while maintaining full resolution of the critical pairs.

Flatten the gradient one duration step to recover the middle-pair resolution lost at the higher starting organic fraction. This tests whether the late pair’s resolution margin can support a fully resolved method faster than injection 9.

Injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark, while higher starting organic fractions showed competing resolution losses at 60 °C. Test the low-temperature selectivity regime with a steeper gradient to look for an alternative, faster fully resolved separation.

Shorten the low-temperature gradient to test whether slope-driven selectivity separates the co-eluting middle pair and reduces elution time. Injection 9 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score fallback.

Test a higher starting organic fraction at 25 °C to shift the competing critical-pair selectivities while shortening retention. Injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark if this alternative cannot achieve full resolution.

Increasing the starting organic fraction improved both critical pairs and shortened elution in injection 14. Test one further increase to see whether that trend can produce a faster fully resolved method, retaining injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction by one grid step to seek full resolution of the remaining R = 1.43 pair while further shortening elution. Monitor the middle cluster for a competing loss of resolution.

Slightly flatten injection 16’s gradient to improve the two under-resolved pairs while using the middle pair’s R = 2.19 margin. This could deliver full resolution with substantially earlier final elution than injection 9.

Injection 17 achieved maximum CRF with the last peak at 4.14 minutes. Increase the endpoint one step to test whether a slightly steeper gradient can shorten elution while keeping the critical R = 1.61 pair fully resolved.

The steeper gradient lost full resolution, so return to injection 17’s gradient and raise temperature one step. This tests whether temperature can shorten the fully resolved separation without sacrificing either critical pair.

Return to 25 °C and test a higher starting organic fraction with a substantially shallower gradient to compensate for the middle-pair selectivity loss. Injection 17 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Lower the starting organic fraction relative to injection 19 to recover the critical middle-pair separation, while retaining the faster 30 °C temperature. This tests a nearby route to full resolution with final elution near or below injection 17’s 4.14 minutes.

Slightly steepen injection 21’s gradient to improve the R = 1.38 middle pair and shorten retention, while testing whether its neighboring pair retains full resolution. Injection 17 remains the fastest fully resolved method.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction moves the critical middle pair through its selectivity crossover into a faster resolved region. Keep injection 17 as the fastest proven maximum-score method and monitor early-peak compression.

Test whether temperature moves the remaining close middle pair beyond its apparent selectivity crossover at this high starting organic fraction. Injection 17 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method if early-peak compression or another crossover limits this faster candidate.

Flatten the gradient substantially around injection 24’s very short elution window to test whether the two remaining close pairs gain full resolution. Retain injection 17 as the fastest proven maximum-CRF method if this final candidate falls short.
